skill.name: Personification
skill.why: Giving things human feelings makes a scene feel alive, friendly or creepy.
skill.how: Find a thing that isn't a person. Is it doing something only people do?

steps.say: Mo's fridge is full of leftovers.

show.nudge: Fridges are real. What is the fridge doing?
Leftovers are just food. Which part is something people do?

steps.ask: Tap the part only a person could really do.
steps.win: Yes! Fridges hum. Only people grumble.

steps.ask: Which bike is doing something only people do?

options.text: The old bike had a flat tyre.
options.reason: Bikes really get flat tyres. That's a bike thing, not a people thing.

options.text: The old bike sulked in the shed.
Mo rode the old bike to the jetty.
options.reason: Mo is a person, so riding is normal for him. Look for a thing acting human.

steps.win: Yes! Bikes can't sulk. A thing acting human is personification.

steps.say: Careful! Animals count too, but only doing a people thing.

show.text: The magpie sang in the gum tree.
show.nudge: Magpies really sing. That's a magpie thing.
Crabs really run sideways. That's a crab thing.

show.text: The magpie gossiped about the neighbours.

steps.win: Yes! Magpies sing, but they can't gossip. Only people gossip.

steps.say: People doing people things don't count either.

show.nudge: The crowd are real people. Cheering is normal for them.
Balls really fly when you kick them. That's not a people thing.

steps.win: Yes! Wind can blow, but it can't tease.

steps.say: Now ask why. Personification shows how a thing seems.

options.reason: Shy people don't scare anyone. Picture someone peeking shyly.
Shy people are quiet. What is a shy person like?

steps.win: Yes! Shy people are gentle. So the moon seems gentle.

steps.say: Change the doing word, and the feeling changes.

show.nudge: Yawning is sleepy, not angry. Which one sounds like someone cross?

show.text: The sea giggled on the sand.
show.nudge: Giggling is happy. Which one sounds like someone cross?

steps.ask: Tap the one that makes the sea seem angry.
steps.win: Yes! Angry people shove. So the sea seems angry.

terms.means: A thing or animal doing something only people do.
Not a person: an object, the weather, or an animal.
The doing word. Something only people do, like grumble, sulk or tease.

card.test: Find a thing that isn't a person. Is its doing word something only people do?

weDo.hint: Which sentence has the bike doing something only people do?
weDo.success: Bikes can't sulk. Only people sulk, so the bike is acting like a person.

parts: Mo's old bike lived in the shed.

parts.tap: It had a flat tyre.
parts.reason: Bikes really get flat tyres. That's not a person thing.

parts.tap: It sulked in the corner all winter.
Mo pumped up the tyre in spring.
parts.reason: Mo is a person, so this is just what he did.

weDo.text: The storm threw a tantrum. It stamped on the roof and slammed the shed door, again and again.
weDo.prompt: How does the personification make the storm seem?
weDo.hint: What kind of person stamps, slams doors and throws a tantrum?
weDo.success: Angry and wild. Tantrums, stamping and slamming doors are what furious people do.

options.reason: Calm people don't stamp and slam doors.
Sad people go quiet. This storm is stamping and slamming.

creature.name: Humbret
creature.blurb: An egret that's sure the whole mangrove forest is alive. It chats with the tide, argues with the wind and says sorry to the mud.

write.ask: Rewrite this sentence so the wind does something only people do. Make the wind seem angry.
given: The wind blew the door shut.
checks: The wind does something only people do
My doing word makes the wind seem angry
write.model: The wind kicked the door shut and stomped off down the jetty.

encounters.frame: Mo is making breakfast. The Humbret is watching from the porthole.
encounters.prompt: Tap the personification.
encounters.success: Toasters can't grumble about early starts. Only people do that, so the toaster is acting like a person.

parts: Mo got up early to make breakfast for the crew. He put two slices of bread in the old toaster.

parts.tap: The toaster grumbled about the early start.
Mo poured six glasses of milk.
parts.reason: Mo is a person, so pouring milk is just what he did.

parts: The milk was a bit lumpy.

parts.tap: Soon the bread turned black.
parts.reason: Bread really turns black when it burns. That's not a person thing.

parts: Smoke filled the galley.

parts.tap: Tully opened all the windows.
parts.reason: Tully is a person, so this is just what she did.

parts: Gus coughed. 'Toast is off,' said Mo. 'Who wants lumpy milk?' Nobody did.

encounters.frame: The crew found an old house at the end of the jetty. The Humbret won't go any closer.
encounters.text: Nobody had lived in the old house for fifty years. The paint was peeling off the walls. Half the roof was missing. The crew stopped at the gate. The dark windows glared at them. The front door creaked open in the wind. Mo grabbed Tully's arm. 'I've just remembered,' he said. 'I left the oven on.' He ran all the way back to the boat. The others were right behind him.
encounters.prompt: How do the glaring windows make the house seem?
encounters.success: Creepy and unfriendly. People glare when they're cross, so the house seems to want them gone.

options.reason: Welcoming people smile. Glaring windows make the crew run away.
Glaring is not sleepy. The house seems cross, and the crew runs.

encounters.frame: Indi wrote a note about Tully's footy report. One word is wrong.
encounters.text: It was a very windy day at the footy. The wind teased the players all game. It snatched the ball out of the air and threw it back the wrong way. It pulled off Tully's cap and rolled it down the field. The crowd laughed. Tully chased her cap for ages. In the end, the Reef Rays won by one point. Tully is still looking for her cap.
encounters.prompt: Tap the word Indi got wrong, then choose a better one.
encounters.success: Wind. The wind teases the players, and teasing is something people do.

parts: The writer makes the

parts.tap: ball

parts: act like a person. It

parts.tap: teased
parts.reason: That's right. The wind teased the players.

parts: the players. It took Tully's

parts.tap: cap
parts.reason: That's right. The wind pulled off her cap.

options.reason: The crowd are real people. Personification makes a thing act like a person.
The cap just blows away. It doesn't do anything a person does.

encounters.frame: The Humbret found this poem pinned to the boardwalk.
encounters.text: Low Tide. In the afternoon, the tide tiptoed out of the bay. It left the mud shiny and wet. Crabs ran sideways over the mud. Gulls pecked at shells. A boy dug for pipis with his toes. His bucket was soon full. Then the sun went down. The boy went home for tea. The crabs went back into their holes.
encounters.prompt: Which thing in the poem acts like a person?
encounters.success: The tide. Tiptoeing is what people do when they sneak out quietly.

options.reason: Crabs really run sideways. That's a crab thing, not a person thing.
Gulls really peck at shells. That's what gulls do.

encounters.frame: Indi is writing about her art studio. The Humbret is sorting her sentences.
encounters.prompt: Put each sentence where it belongs.
encounters.success: Things acting like people is personification. People and animals doing their own things is not.

items.text: The paintbrush danced across the page.
items.reason: A brush can't dance. Only people dance like that.

items.text: The sun smiled through the window.
items.reason: The sun can't smile. Smiling is a person thing.

items.text: The paint tubes argued about the last spot in the box.
items.reason: Paint tubes can't argue. Only people argue.

items.text: Indi washed her brushes.
items.reason: Indi is a person, so this is just what she did.

items.text: The paint dried in an hour.
items.reason: Paint really dries. That's not a person thing.

items.text: The cat knocked over a jar of water.
items.reason: Cats really knock things over. That's a cat thing.

encounters.frame: Tully is telling the crew about her uncle's old ute. The Humbret is giggling.
encounters.text: My uncle Pete has a very old ute. It is rusty and orange. It has done hundreds of trips to the beach. But it hates hills. Every time we get to a hill, the ute sulks at the bottom. The engine roars, but the wheels don't turn. We all have to get out and push. Uncle Pete says it's a good workout. Aunty Jo says it's time for a new ute.
encounters.prompt: What does 'the ute sulks at the bottom' tell you?
encounters.success: It stops and won't go, like a sulky kid. That's why everyone has to get out and push.

options.reason: Utes can't feel sad. What does a sulky kid do when you ask them to move?
If it zoomed, nobody would need to push. Why are they pushing it?

encounters.frame: Wren found her old camping diary. The Humbret is reading it by torchlight.
encounters.text: Camp diary, first night. We set up our tents in a paddock miles from any town. There were no street lights at all, so when the sun went down, it got really dark. I'll be honest: I was a bit nervous. Then the Moon peeked over the hill. It climbed slowly into the sky, and it kept watch over our tents all night. Every time I woke up, it was still there, shining through the tent flap. I stopped worrying and slept better than I do at home. In the morning, Dad asked if the possums had kept me awake. I didn't even hear them.
encounters.prompt: How does the personification make the Moon seem?
encounters.success: Kind and protective. People keep watch to keep others safe, and Wren stops worrying because of it.

options.text: lonely and sad, all by itself in the sky
options.reason: Nothing says the Moon is sad. It keeps watch, and Wren feels safe.

options.text: kind and protective, looking after the campers
scary and sneaky, spying on the tents
options.reason: Wren stops worrying because the Moon is there. It feels safe, not scary.

encounters.frame: Zed dug his old console out of a box. The Humbret is pressing buttons with its beak.
encounters.prompt: Tap the personification.
encounters.success: Consoles can't complain. Only people complain, so the old console is acting like a grumpy person.

parts: On Saturday, Zed found his very first games console in a box under his bed. It was covered in dust and stickers. He plugged it into the TV and blew on the cartridge for luck.

parts.tap: The old console complained loudly every time Zed pressed start.

parts: After the fourth try, the screen flickered and the music began.

parts.tap: Zed's character, a tiny knight, ran across the castle bridge.
parts.reason: The knight is a person in the game, so running isn't personification.

parts.tap: The music sounded like a doorbell on fast forward.
parts.reason: This compares the music to a doorbell using like. It's a simile.

parts: Zed played until he reached the dragon on level two.

parts.tap: The dragon breathed fire across the screen.
parts.reason: Dragons breathe fire in stories. That's a dragon thing, not a person thing.

parts: Zed's knight was burnt to a crisp in two seconds. 'I used to be so good at this,' he said.

encounters.frame: Gus wrote a note about Wren's picnic story. One word is wrong.
encounters.text: It was the hottest day of the year, and we had our picnic on the beach anyway. By lunchtime, the sun glared down at us from a cloudless sky. There was no shade anywhere. The birthday cake gave up and slumped sideways, and its pink icing slid onto the rug. The lemonade went warm. A line of ants crawled across the sand towards the food. Mum put up a beach umbrella, but the wind blew it into the water. In the end, we ate warm, squashed cake in the car with the air-conditioning on full blast. It was still the best birthday ever.
encounters.prompt: Tap the part Gus got wrong, then choose a better one.
encounters.success: Cruel. Glaring is an angry stare, not a curious one, so the sun seems fierce on this scorching day.

parts: In Wren's story, the

parts.tap: sun
parts.reason: That's right. In Wren's story, the sun glared down from a cloudless sky.

parts: glares down at the picnic. That makes it seem

parts.tap: curious

parts: . The

parts.tap: cake
parts.reason: That's right. The cake 'gave up and slumped sideways' in the heat.

parts: gives up and slumps, so it seems worn out.

options.reason: Sleepy people doze. This sun glares so hard there's no shade anywhere.
Shy people look away. This sun stares down all day from a cloudless sky.

encounters.frame: Poet Pip wrote these lines about a school band. The Humbret is sorting them.
encounters.prompt: Put each line where it belongs.
encounters.success: Instruments that sulk, gossip or giggle are acting like people. Birds singing and drummers counting are not.

items.text: The guitar sulked in its case after the show.
items.reason: A guitar can't sulk. Sulking is a person thing.

items.text: The drums gossiped with the cymbals at the back.
items.reason: Drums can't gossip. Only people gossip.

items.text: The trumpet giggled at the tuba's jokes.
items.reason: A trumpet can't giggle or get a joke. Giggling is a person thing.

items.text: The magpies sang in the gum tree outside.
items.reason: Magpies really sing. That's a bird thing, not personification.

items.text: The drummer counted to four, then started.
items.reason: The drummer is a person, so this is just what he did.

items.text: The lights went off after the last song.
items.reason: Lights really do go off. Nothing here acts like a person.

items.text: The crowd clapped and cheered for ages.
items.reason: The crowd are real people, so clapping is just what they did.

encounters.frame: Wren is writing up a night-time rescue. The Humbret is keeping the joey warm.
encounters.text: The phone rang at ten o'clock. A mother kangaroo was lying by the highway, too hurt to move, and there was a joey in her pouch. I grabbed my rescue bag and a torch and drove out. The wind was angry that night. It shoved against my car doors and flung leaves at my windscreen. A vet was already looking after the mother, so the joey was mine to care for. It was shaking and squeaking with fright. I wrapped it in a pillowcase and held it against my chest. My torch kept flickering, so I worked mostly by feel. By midnight, the joey was asleep in a warm basket in my kitchen.
encounters.prompt: Which thing in Wren's story is given a human mood?
encounters.success: The wind. Anger is a human mood, and this wind shoves and flings like a cross person.

options.reason: Joeys really get scared and squeak. That's an animal feeling, not personification.
Torches really flicker when the battery is low. That's not a person thing.

encounters.frame: Gus wrote this about the ship's fridge. The Humbret has seen inside it and wishes it hadn't.
encounters.text: The Soggy Biscuit's fridge has had enough of us. It is older than Tully, and it is full of my science experiments: a jar of fish guts, three tubs of mould, and a slime that may be alive. Every time someone opens the door, the fridge lets out a long, slow groan. Most mornings, it refuses to close until somebody kicks it. Last week it gave up completely and dripped all over the floor. Mo says it's just old. I think it's sick of my fish guts. To be fair, so is everyone else. Tomorrow I'm moving the fish guts to a bucket on deck. The fridge has earned a rest.
encounters.prompt: How does the personification make the fridge seem?
encounters.success: Tired and fed up. Groaning, refusing and giving up are what worn-out, fed-up people do.

options.reason: Helpful people don't refuse to do their job. This fridge groans and gives up.
Gus says the fridge is older than Tully. It seems worn out.

encounters.frame: Tully read this from an old fisherman's logbook. The Humbret is clinging to the mast.
encounters.text: We left the harbour at dawn, and for two hours the water was flat and grey. Then the wind swung around to the south. The sea complained under the boat for the rest of the trip, and it never once let up. Grey waves rose and fell beside us, higher each hour. A flock of gulls fought over a fish head on the back deck. My brother complained about the weather, then went very quiet and gripped the wheel with both hands. Nobody made jokes. Nobody even tried to eat the sandwiches. It took us six hours to get back, a trip that usually takes two. When we finally tied up at the jetty, I sat down on a crate and didn't move for a long time. We didn't catch a single fish, and I have never been so glad to see dry land.
encounters.prompt: Which line from the log is personification?
encounters.success: Only people complain. The brother is a person, so his complaint is plain. The sea complaining is personification.

options.text: A flock of gulls fought over a fish head on the back deck.
options.reason: Gulls really fight over scraps. That's a bird thing, not a people thing.

options.text: Grey waves rose and fell beside us, higher each hour.
options.reason: Waves really rise and fall. Nothing here acts like a person.

options.text: My brother complained about the weather.
options.reason: The brother is a person. Complaining is just what people do.

options.text: The sea complained under the boat for the rest of the trip.

encounters.frame: Tully is writing up the Reef Rays' unluckiest game of the year. The Humbret couldn't bear to watch.
encounters.prompt: Tully wants you to feel the Rays had terrible luck. Tap the personification that does that.
encounters.success: Posts can't jump on purpose. They seem to be blocking the Rays, so the team's luck feels terrible.

parts: The Reef Rays needed one win to make the finals, and the whole town came to watch.

parts.tap: The sun smiled down on the packed stands.
parts.reason: A smiling sun makes the day feel cheerful. It says nothing about the Rays' luck.

parts: We kicked two early goals, and the crowd went wild. Then the Pinchers hit back, goal after goal. In the last quarter, we finally had our chances.

parts.tap: The posts seemed to jump in front of every kick we took.

parts: Shot after shot bounced off the wood.

parts.tap: The old grandstand groaned as two thousand people stood up.
parts.reason: This shows how big and heavy the crowd was. It isn't about luck.

parts: We lost by four points. We sat on the bench afterwards, and nobody said a word.

parts.tap: Then the rain politely waited until we had packed the kit bags.
parts.reason: Waiting politely is kind. The rain seems to help the team, not spoil things.

parts: It poured the moment the last bag was in the bus. Next week we play the Pinchers again, and Coach says we'll be ready. She has already bought a new whistle.

encounters.frame: Zed wrote notes about a ghost story from the Mirage Mangroves library. One word is wrong.
encounters.text: Ava had walked the mangrove track a hundred times in the daytime, but never after dark. Tonight she had no choice: the last ferry had gone, and the only way home was through the trees. At first, it wasn't too bad. Then the track narrowed, and the mangroves crowded in on both sides. Their branches reached for her hair and snagged her sleeves. The roots crept across the track to trip her up. Behind her, the leaves whispered to one another, and she was sure they were whispering about her. Ava walked faster. She was shaking now, and she kept her eyes fixed on the little patch of torchlight in front of her. Twice, the trees seemed to close the path completely, and she had to push through. When she finally saw the lights of her street, she ran the last hundred metres. She didn't stop until the front door was locked behind her.
encounters.prompt: Tap the word Zed got wrong, then choose a better one.
encounters.success: Gossipy. People who whisper about someone are gossiping, so the leaves seem to be talking about Ava.

parts: The leaves whispering about Ava make them seem

parts.tap: cheerful

parts: . The branches that reach for her hair seem

parts.tap: grabby
parts.reason: Grabby fits. Branches that reach for her hair and snag her sleeves seem to grab at her.

parts: . The roots that creep across the track seem

parts.tap: sneaky
parts.reason: Sneaky fits. The roots creep across the track to trip her up.

options.reason: Shy people whisper because they're nervous. These leaves whisper about Ava, and it frightens her.
Sleepy things are quiet, but these leaves are busy whispering about Ava behind her back.
Kind people don't whisper about you behind your back. Ava walks faster to get away.

encounters.frame: Indi has labelled her sketches of the Mirage Mangroves. The Humbret is checking her work.
encounters.prompt: Put each caption where it belongs.
encounters.success: Things doing people things is personification. Animals doing animal things isn't, even when the word sounds human.

items.text: The old jetty grumbled about the cold every winter.
items.reason: A jetty can't grumble about the weather. Only people do that.

items.text: Two pelicans squabbled over a fish head on the jetty.
items.reason: Pelicans really fight over food. That's a bird thing, not personification.

items.text: The mudflats gleamed like a pair of polished school shoes.
items.reason: This compares the mud to shoes using like. It's a simile.

items.text: The clouds hurried across the sky, late for a meeting.
items.reason: Clouds can't be late for meetings. They're acting like busy people.

items.text: A crab raised one claw as a gull came close.
items.reason: Crabs really raise their claws to scare birds off. That's a crab thing.

items.text: The mangrove roots were a tangle of grey spaghetti.
items.reason: This says the roots ARE spaghetti, with no like or as. That's a metaphor.

items.text: The mangroves held hands all along the riverbank.
items.reason: Trees can't hold hands. Only people do that.

encounters.frame: Gus is testing his new robot vacuum. The Humbret is watching from the bench.
encounters.prompt: Which sentence makes the robot vacuum seem nervous?
encounters.success: Nervous. A nervous person peeks at something scary, then hides. The vacuum does both.

options.text: The vacuum marched across the rug, bossing the crumbs about.
options.reason: Marching and bossing make it seem bossy and sure of itself, not nervous.

options.text: The vacuum sulked after Gus kicked it.
options.reason: Sulking shows it's cross with Gus, not scared of anything.

options.text: The vacuum peeked at the dog, then hid again.
The vacuum gobbled the crumbs, then burped with pride.
options.reason: Gobbling and burping with pride make it seem greedy and pleased with itself.

encounters.frame: Mo wrote this for the crew newsletter. The Humbret thinks Mo might be the problem.
encounters.text: My alarm clock hates me. I'm serious. Every night I set it for six o'clock, because breakfast for six people doesn't cook itself. And every morning, at exactly six o'clock, it shrieks right next to my ear until I sit bolt upright. I have tried everything. I put it under my pillow. I put it in my sock drawer. I even put it in the fridge, but that just made it cold and cross. Tully says it's a perfectly good clock that does exactly what I ask it to do. Gus says it's much louder than it needs to be, and he'd know, because his bunk is next to mine. Zed offered to reprogram it to play a gentle song instead, but I said no. If I'm getting up at six, that clock is getting up at six too. Tomorrow I'm making porridge. The clock doesn't get any. Gus says I'm the one who needs reprogramming. We'll see who's laughing then.
encounters.prompt: Why does Mo say his alarm clock hates him?
encounters.success: It wakes him up early every day, and that feels mean. So Mo talks about it like a nasty person.

options.text: It is broken and keeps ringing at the wrong time.
options.reason: Tully says it does exactly what he asks. It rings at six, just as he sets it.

options.text: It wakes him up early every day, which feels mean.
It is too quiet and never manages to wake him.
options.reason: Mo says it shrieks next to his ear until he sits bolt upright. It's not quiet.

options.text: Mo dropped it once, and it has been angry ever since.
options.reason: Mo never says he dropped it. It 'hates' him because it wakes him so early.

encounters.frame: The Soggy Biscuit's radio picked up this blog from a space scientist. The Humbret is listening carefully.
encounters.text: For six years, my team has driven a little rover called Pebble across the surface of Mars, sending it instructions from a control room on the other side of the solar system. Pebble was only built to last ninety days. Nobody told Pebble. When its left wheel jammed in year two, it taught itself to drive backwards, dragging the broken wheel behind it. When a dust storm blotted out the sun for a month, Pebble switched off everything except its heater and waited patiently in the dark, all on its own, until the sky cleared. Every evening, at the end of its work, it sent us a photo of the Martian sunset, as if it were saying goodnight to the people who built it. Last week, the dust finally won. Pebble's solar panels were too dirty to charge, and its last message reached us on Tuesday morning: a picture of a small grey rock, and the words BATTERY LOW. Half the control room cried. The other half pretended they had dust in their eyes. We still send Pebble a message every evening, just in case it wakes up. Its little wheel tracks are still there in the red dust, and they will be for a very long time.
encounters.prompt: Why does the scientist write about Pebble as if it were a person?
encounters.success: To make you care. Pebble taught itself, waited patiently and said goodnight, so losing it feels like losing a friend.

options.text: So readers learn how a rover's solar panels and wheels work.
options.reason: The blog mentions panels, but 'taught itself' and 'saying goodnight' aren't about how parts work.

options.text: So readers care about Pebble, like a friend they have lost.
So readers believe Pebble really could think and feel lonely.
options.reason: That's taking it literally. The scientist knows Pebble is a machine.

options.text: So readers see that Pebble was badly built and broke too soon.
options.reason: Pebble was built for ninety days and lasted six years. It did far better than planned.

encounters.frame: Mo entered a cooking competition. The Humbret is the only one brave enough to taste his dish.
encounters.prompt: Tap the personification where the story turns from hopeful to embarrassing.
encounters.success: Scones that slink out ashamed seem embarrassed. Before that, the oven and spoon made everything sound hopeful.

parts: The Mirage Mangroves Bake-Off was held in the community hall, and Mo had entered his famous gum-leaf scones. The crew had asked him, very politely, not to.

parts.tap: The big oven hummed a happy tune as it warmed up.
parts.reason: A happy tune makes things sound hopeful. Nothing has gone wrong yet.

parts: Mo measured everything twice and still got it wrong.

parts.tap: His wooden spoon cheered him on with every stir.
parts.reason: A spoon cheering Mo on makes him seem ready to win. It's still hopeful here.

parts: He shaped twelve scones, slid the tray into the oven and waited.

parts.tap: Twenty minutes later, the scones slunk out of the oven, grey and ashamed.

parts: The other bakers looked at the tray and then looked away. The head judge, Mrs Okafor, tapped one scone with her spoon. It made a sound like a door knocker. She tried a crumb and chewed for a very long time.

parts.tap: Her pen hurried across the clipboard while she reached for a glass of water.
parts.reason: The pen is busy because the judge is writing. The scones let Mo down before this.

parts: Then she asked for another glass. Mo came last, but he got a special certificate for Most Unusual Flavour. He has framed it and hung it above the stove. Mrs Okafor has asked him to bring something different next year. Mo is already planning a gum-leaf pavlova, and nobody is brave enough to stop him.

encounters.frame: Gus wrote a note about Poet Pip's piano story. One word is wrong.
encounters.text: The piano had stood in the corner of the Mangrove Point hall for nearly eighty years, and for most of that time nobody had played it. Its lid was scratched, two of its keys were missing, and a family of spiders had moved into the space behind the pedals. Children ran past it on their way to the toilets. Every Christmas, someone would hang tinsel on it and then forget it was there until February. The piano watched them all go by and waited. Then, one rainy Saturday, a new girl called Mira wandered in while her mum set up for the craft market. She lifted the lid, brushed off a cobweb and pressed one key, then another. The piano cleared its throat with a dusty, wheezing note. Mira kept going. By the third song, people at the market had stopped to listen, and by the fourth, a small crowd had gathered round. The old piano sang for her, as if it had been saving every song for eighty years. When Mira finally closed the lid, everyone clapped. The hall committee had the piano tuned the following week. Mira plays it every Saturday now, and the spiders have moved out. Most of them.
encounters.prompt: Tap the word Gus got wrong, then choose a better one.
encounters.success: Joyful. It sings 'as if it had been saving every song for eighty years', like someone thrilled to perform.

parts: Singing for Mira makes the piano seem

parts.tap: annoyed

parts: . Watching and waiting for eighty years makes it seem

parts.tap: patient
parts.reason: Patient fits. It watched and waited for years without anyone playing it.

parts: . Clearing its throat with a dusty note makes it seem

encounters.frame: Wren wrote this for the Mirage Mangroves rescue centre newsletter. Her first draft was much plainer.
encounters.text: After four months at the rescue centre, Crumpet the green turtle was finally ready to go home. She had come to us in winter, tangled in fishing line and far too thin, and it had taken weeks of care and a great many squid before she was strong enough to swim properly again. On release day, six of us carried her down to the beach in a padded crate, while a small crowd gathered on the sand. The morning was calm and bright. As we set the crate down at the edge of the water, the sea opened its arms to her. Gentle waves rolled up the sand, curled around her flippers and coaxed her forward, as if the whole sea had been waiting for her to come home. Crumpet paused for a moment and lifted her head. Then she pushed off into the shallows, and the water folded itself softly around her shell. A few seconds later, she surfaced once, took a breath and was gone. Nobody on the beach said anything for a while. Then the youngest volunteer, who had fed Crumpet every morning, burst into happy tears. We will miss her, but she is exactly where she belongs.
encounters.prompt: Wren's first draft said only 'Gentle waves rolled up the sand.' Why did she add 'the sea opened its arms to her'?
encounters.success: Open arms are how families greet someone coming home. The sea seems glad to have Crumpet back.

options.text: It makes the sea feel like a strong giant, dragging Crumpet into the deep.
options.reason: Open arms are gentle, not strong. The morning is calm, and the waves coax her forward.

options.text: It makes the sea feel like family, hugging Crumpet as she comes home.
It shows Crumpet swam with her flippers spread wide like arms.
options.reason: It's the sea that opens its arms, not Crumpet. It tells you how the sea seems.

options.text: It makes the sea feel like a sad friend, reaching out to say goodbye.
options.reason: Open arms are a welcome, not a goodbye. It's the volunteers who will miss her.

encounters.frame: Gus's mum sent him a letter. Gus read it out to the crew, who all agreed with his mum.
encounters.text: Dear Gus, I hope life on the Soggy Biscuit is going well and that you are remembering to wash behind your ears. I am writing about the sock. You know the one. It is grey, it used to be white, and you hid it under your bed before you left for the summer, along with half a cheese sandwich. Well, on Thursday morning the sock crawled out from under your bed by itself, dragged itself down the hallway and begged me to wash it. It left a trail of something green on the carpet. The cat took one look at it and moved in with the neighbours, and she has not come back. Your dad tried to pick it up with the barbecue tongs, and the sock wriggled out of the tongs and refused to go in the bin. In the end, I put it in the washing machine on the hottest setting and washed it four times. It came out a lovely pale grey. I have put it in a sealed jar on your shelf, because I know how you feel about your collections. Please never do this again. Love, Mum. PS The cheese sandwich is still missing. If you know where it is, please tell me before the neighbours' cat finds it.
encounters.prompt: Why does Mum make the sock crawl out and beg to be washed?
encounters.success: To show how disgusting it had become. Even the sock seems desperate to be clean.

options.text: To show that the sock had become alive and dangerous.
options.reason: That's taking it literally. Socks can't crawl. Mum is joking about how filthy it was.

options.text: To show that Gus forgot where he put his socks.
options.reason: Mum says Gus hid the sock on purpose. The begging shows how filthy it was.

options.text: To show how filthy and disgusting the sock had become.
To show that the cat had been playing with the sock.
options.reason: The cat ran away from the sock. The begging shows the sock needed washing badly.
